title: The monkey gardeners
hookLine: monkeys water the saplings by pulling each one up to check its roots (Jataka 46)

cards: There's a festival in the city of Benares, crowds in every street, and the king's gardener badly wants to go. But the young trees in the royal park need water while he's away.
A troop of monkeys lives in the park; they eat the fruit and enjoy the shade, so surely they owe him a favor. He goes to their king and asks. The monkey king says: of course.

teach.h: THE GARDENER GOES TO THE FESTIVAL.
teach.b: First, the job. The gardener hands over the water skins and wooden pots and goes off to the festival. The monkey king tells his troop to water the young trees.
Second, the plan. But water is precious, the monkey king says. We mustn't waste it.

teach.h: CHECK THE ROOTS, SAVE THE WATER.
teach.b: So before you water a tree, pull it up and look at its roots. Long roots get a lot; short roots get a little. It's careful, thrifty, and sounds like good management.
Third, the result. The monkeys go through the park, pulling each sapling out of the ground, inspecting the roots, and watering accordingly.
Every young tree they check, they kill. Fourth, the witness. A wise man walking through the park, the bodhisatta in this tale, asks what they're doing.
And he says, in a verse, that the ignorant, trying to do good, do harm instead, like the monkeys in the king's garden. What makes the tale sharp is that nobody is wicked.
The monkeys aren't lazy or greedy. They're conscientious. They wanted to be sure, and being sure meant digging up the very thing that needed to stay in the dark to grow.
A root does its work out of sight.

how: Buddhist teachers tell the Aramadusaka Jataka as a lesson that good intentions need wisdom too, and that checking too soon can do harm.

o: careful and eager to do the job right
lazy and looking for a shortcut
greedy for a bigger share of fruit

games.q: the monkey gardeners: tap the pairs.
p: left for the festival in the city
said pull them up to check the roots
said the ignorant harm while helping

s: the monkeys ruined the garden because they were lazy
they were careful and thrifty; the method was the problem.
the monkey king's plan was meant to save water
he told them to measure each tree's roots so no water was wasted.
the wise man in the park is the bodhisatta
he sees the monkeys at work and speaks the verse about harm done while trying to help.

games.q: you're a monkey with a water skin and a park full of saplings. your king says water is precious. how do you water the trees?
o: water each one a little and leave it.
pull each one up, check the roots, water to match.
skip the small ones and save water for the big ones.
games.why: the monkeys pull every sapling up to check it, and every one they check dies.

practice: Hold in mind something young in your life: a plan, a friendship, a skill, someone you're helping along.
If you've been pulling it up to check its roots, measuring it, asking if it's working yet, picture setting it back in the ground and patting the soil down. Water it, leave it alone, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Conscientious. What the monkey gardeners were, careful helpers who pulled up every sapling to measure its roots, and killed what they meant to save. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: don't pull up the roots. Good intentions need wisdom too. Until next time.
